ingredients.name: Raw green mangoes (firm, unripe)
ingredients.notes: washed and cut into quarters or large chunks, skin left on -- the peel softens during cooking and is traditionally eaten

ingredients.name: Sugar
ingredients.notes: balances the sourness of the green mango

ingredients.name: Salt
ingredients.notes: to taste; the mango's natural sourness means less salt is needed than for other curries

steps.instruction: Wash the mangoes well. Do NOT peel them -- the skin softens during cooking and is eaten in Sri Lanka. Cut each mango into quarters, removing the seed, or into large chunks.
Heat the coconut oil in a pan over medium heat. Add mustard seeds and let them splutter. Add fenugreek, curry leaves, and pandan leaf. Sizzle for 30 seconds.
Add the sliced onion, garlic, and green chillies. Saute until the onion softens, about 3 minutes.
Add the turmeric, chilli powder, and curry powder. Stir for 30 seconds.
Add the mango pieces and toss to coat in the spice base. Add the sugar and salt.
Pour in the thin coconut milk. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover, and cook for 15-18 minutes until the mango is tender and the skin is soft. Stir gently occasionally to avoid breaking the mango pieces.

Add the thick coconut milk. Stir gently and simmer uncovered for 3-5 minutes until the gravy thickens. Taste and adjust the balance of salt, sweetness, and sourness -- green mango varies widely in sourness, so adjustments are often needed.
Serve hot with red rice, alongside a mild dhal curry and pol sambol for a classic village-style meal.

source_site: islandsmile.org, cross-checked against foodcnr.com, cookingandme.com, sbs.com.au (O Tama Carey), greatbritishchefs.com (Kolamba), and preethicuisine.com
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 6+ independent sources including two professional Sri Lankan restaurant chefs (O Tama Carey and Kolamba's Eroshan Meewella); strong agreement on keeping the skin on and using thin-then-thick coconut milk
notes: Amba maluwa (mango curry) is unique in Sri Lankan cooking because it uses a fruit that acts like a vegetable -- the natural sourness of unripe green mango replaces goraka or tamarind as the souring agent, making this curry both sour and savoury simultaneously. Cooking with the skin on is explicitly described by multiple Sri Lankan sources (including islandsmile.org and sbs.com.au's recipe from chef O Tama Carey) as the correct traditional approach -- the skin softens completely during cooking and adds flavour and colour to the gravy. The sugar in the recipe is not optional -- it is needed to balance the intense natural sourness of the green mango. The exact amount of sugar needed will vary depending on the ripeness and variety of the mango; always taste and adjust after the initial simmer.
